start.text:
The triage desk calls you to bay 4. Fatima Al-Rashid, 32 years old, 31 weeks and 5 days pregnant, has arrived by ambulance.

She is gripping the side-rail of the trolley, bent forward, face contorted. 'My stomach — it started really suddenly, about an hour ago. The pain just keeps going, it won't ease off at all.'

Her partner, Mohammed, stands at the entrance: 'She was standing in the kitchen when it hit her. She doubled over. The floor had blood on it when we left.'

The paramedic hands you the observations:
HR 118 | BP 138/92 | RR 22 | Temp 37.0°C | SpO₂ 97%

'We tried the Doppler twice,' the paramedic adds, lowering their voice. 'We couldn't get a fetal heartbeat.'

The community midwife steps beside you: 'I know Fatima — she's G2P1, had a normal delivery at 39 weeks four years ago. Chronic hypertension, well-controlled on labetalol 100mg twice daily. Her last clinic BP was 132/84 two weeks ago. She's been completely uncomplicated this pregnancy.'

Fatima's hands feel cold. Her abdomen is visibly gravid. She looks frightened.

What is your immediate response?

choices.text: OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY — call the OB team right now. Insert 2 large-bore IVs. Apply CTG immediately. Draw urgent bloods: CBC, coagulation screen, group and save, lactate. Don't move her until monitoring is running.

Coagulation screen ordered — essential to detect developing DIC in the setting of major haemorrhage
Group and save sent — blood group and crossmatch are critical before theatre and blood product administration

premature-history.text:
You begin to take a structured history. Fatima is struggling to answer between grimaces. Mohammed fills in the details — sudden onset while standing, approximately 75 minutes ago, no trauma, bleeding started about 40 minutes in, dark red, baby has felt 'quiet all afternoon'.

The midwife interrupts you firmly: 'I'm sorry — I need to stop you. I've tried the Doppler twice. I cannot get a fetal heartbeat. We need monitoring on this baby right now. The history can wait.'

She's right.

choices.text: Apply CTG and complete the clinical assessment immediately

uss-done-first.text:
The portable ultrasound is wheeled in. The on-call sonographer scans Fatima's abdomen.

Findings:
• Placenta: posterior, appearing thickened and heterogeneous (~5.5cm)
• Possible hypoechoic collection behind the posterior placental margin — approximately 4×3cm — NOT definitively diagnostic
• Fetal cardiac activity: present, rate approximately 80–88 bpm ← BRADYCARDIC (reference 110–160 at 31+5)
• Fetal position: cephalic, liquor volume appears reduced

Sonographer: 'I can see something that might be a retroplacental haematoma but I can't be sure. The resolution isn't clear enough. I cannot rule abruption in or out.'

[!] CLINICAL TEACHING: Ultrasound sensitivity for placental abruption is only 24–48%. In one major series, half of confirmed abruptions were missed on USS. A normal or non-diagnostic USS does NOT rule out abruption. Clinical diagnosis is primary — USS is not the right tool for this question.

[!] The fetal bradycardia seen on USS confirms the picture but 25 minutes have passed with no electronic fetal monitoring applied to this baby.

Electronic fetal monitoring is the most urgent outstanding step.

choices.text: Apply CTG and proceed with full clinical assessment

initial-assessment.text:
You perform a rapid structured clinical assessment:

GENERAL: Fatima is pale and diaphoretic. Her hands are cold and clammy. Capillary refill 3 seconds. She cannot complete sentences during pain.

ABDOMEN:
→ Fundal height: 31cm — appropriate for gestation
→ Uterine consistency: BOARD-LIKE RIGIDITY. The uterus feels hard as wood and does not relax between assessments. This is NOT labour — contractions relax. This uterus does not relax.
→ Tenderness: Exquisite tenderness to even light palpation over the entire uterus, worst at the fundus
→ There are no discrete contraction waves

PER VAGINAM ASSESSMENT: Approximately 150–200mL dark, deoxygenated blood noted on the pad. Not bright red. This dark colouration is consistent with blood that has tracked from a retroplacental haematoma rather than fresh active bleeding from the placental edge.

FETAL DOPPLER: 77 bpm. Fetal bradycardia (reference: 110–160 bpm at 31+5 weeks).

COMPLETED HISTORY:
• Pain: Constant, severe, sudden onset 75 minutes ago while stationary — not periodic, does not come and go
• Bleeding: Started 40 minutes ago — dark, not bright red
• Fetal movements: Baby has been quiet all afternoon
• Medications: Labetalol 100mg BD for chronic hypertension. No NSAIDs. No anticoagulants.
• Allergies: NKDA
• Blood group: Unknown — not in handheld notes

CLINICAL IMPRESSION: Sudden-onset severe constant abdominal pain + dark vaginal bleeding + board-like hypertonic uterus + fetal bradycardia in a 31+5-week pregnancy = PLACENTAL ABRUPTION. This is the diagnosis until proven otherwise, and this baby needs delivering.

How do you proceed?

choices.text: Placental abruption — this is a Category 1 emergency. CTG NOW if not applied. Call OB emergency if not done. IV access ×2. Bloods: CBC, coag screen, group and save, lactate.

bloods-only-result.text:
The blood results return 45 minutes later. While waiting, you notice Fatima has become increasingly restless. You try the Doppler again — fetal heart rate 72 bpm.

Blood Results:

Haemoglobin: 7.9 g/dL [↓↓] — significantly anaemic. Her booking Hb was 11.4 g/dL. This represents approximately 30% loss of circulating blood volume. Haemodynamic compromise is imminent or already occurring.

Platelets: 82 ×10⁹/L [↓↓] — thrombocytopenic. Trend is critical.

Coagulation Screen:
  INR: 2.3 [↑↑] — severely elevated (reference <1.3)
  APTT: 2.1× upper limit — prolonged
  Fibrinogen: 0.8 g/L [↓↓] — CRITICALLY LOW (reference >2.0 g/L in pregnancy)

⚠ ESTABLISHED DIC — this patient has disseminated intravascular coagulation. The coagulopathy will worsen with every minute until blood products are given and the source (the abruption) is removed.

Lactate: 4.8 mmol/L [↑↑] — severe tissue hypoperfusion.

Group and Save: Blood group B positive. No antibodies. Crossmatch in progress.

BP is now 104/68 (falling from 138/92). HR 138. She is decompensating.

[!] TEACHING: The 45-minute wait for blood results allowed DIC to develop. Electronic fetal monitoring — not haematology — is the investigation that drives the delivery decision in this scenario. A Category III CTG mandates delivery regardless of blood results. Blood products should run in parallel with the decision to deliver, not before it.

CTG has not yet been applied. This must happen now.

choices.text: Apply CTG immediately — fetal assessment cannot wait any longer

effects.reason: CTG applied — though late, electronic fetal monitoring is now established

ctg-result.text:
The CTG trace runs.

FETAL HEART RATE ANALYSIS:
  Baseline: 72–82 bpm — SEVERE FETAL BRADYCARDIA (reference 110–160)
  Baseline variability: < 5 bpm — ABSENT (reference: 5–25 bpm)
  Accelerations: NONE
  Decelerations: Late decelerations with each mild uterine tightening
  Uterine activity: Hypertonic — uterus fails to relax

FIGO CLASSIFICATION: CATEGORY III — PATHOLOGICAL
This CTG requires immediate delivery. There is no threshold of intrauterine resuscitation that is appropriate to attempt first. Category III with severe bradycardia in the context of clinical abruption means: deliver now.

Blood results (if ordered):
  Hb: 8.4 g/dL [↓] — significant haemorrhage (booking Hb 11.4)
  Plt: 96 ×10⁹/L [↓] — falling, watch closely
  INR: 1.8 [↑] — early coagulopathy, DIC developing
  APTT: 1.6× normal [↑] — prolonged
  Fibrinogen: 1.4 g/L [↓] — approaching critical threshold (<1.5 in OB)
  Lactate: 3.2 mmol/L [↑] — tissue hypoperfusion
  Blood group: B positive (if group and save sent)

Current vitals: HR 134, BP 112/74 — blood pressure is falling. Fatima's chronic hypertension means her 'normal' is higher; 112/74 represents significant relative hypotension in this context.

Mohammed is at the door: 'Please — is my baby okay?'

You need to act.

choices.text: Try intrauterine resuscitation first — left lateral position, high-flow oxygen, rapid IV fluid bolus. Give the fetus 10 minutes to respond before committing to theatre.

resuscitation-attempt.text:
You position Fatima in the full left lateral position, apply high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask, and run in 500mL of Hartmann's solution rapidly through the IV.

The CTG continues to run. Ten minutes pass.

The trace does not improve.

Baseline FHR: 68 bpm. Absent variability. The late decelerations have deepened.

BP has dropped further: 96/62. HR 142. Fatima is barely responsive to verbal commands.

The midwife: 'The uterus is not relaxing at all. This isn't labour. This is abruption. The baby is running out of time.'

The obstetric registrar, who has just arrived, looks at the CTG for 4 seconds: 'Emergency CS. Right now. How long has this trace been like this?'

management-hub.text:
CATEGORY 1 CAESAREAN SECTION — DECISION CONFIRMED.

Theatre is being prepared. The anaesthesia team is assembling. You have approximately 5 minutes to ensure everything is in place before Fatima goes through those doors.

Current status:
  HR: 138 | BP: 108/70 | SpO₂: 95% | Consciousness: alert but deteriorating
  Blood group: B positive (if obtained)
  Haemoglobin (if bloods taken): ~8–8.4 g/dL with developing coagulopathy
  Fetal HR on CTG: 70–78 bpm — persistent bradycardia

GESTATIONAL CONTEXT: 31+5 weeks. A ventilated neonate is expected. The survival rate for babies born at 31+5 weeks is >95% with good neonatal care — but that team must be there.

UK MASSIVE HAEMORRHAGE PROTOCOL (MHP) TRIGGERS: Any of the following:
✓ Obstetric haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise
✓ Estimated blood loss >1500mL
✓ Placental abruption requiring emergency delivery

All three are met. What is your complete pre-theatre management?

choices.text: ACTIVATE MHP — 4 units O-negative pRBC running now, 4 units FFP concurrently, platelets requested if Plt <75. Call neonatal team to theatre. Anaesthetics: GA for speed. Obtain verbal consent from Fatima. Blood bank on direct line.

observation-delay.text:
You decide to wait for the blood results.

Fifteen minutes pass.

The CTG alarm sounds — the trace has flatlined. The midwife cannot detect any fetal cardiac activity. Fatima's BP: 72/44. HR: 158. She is pale, cold, and barely responsive.

Blood results finally return: Hb 6.2 g/dL. INR >4. Fibrinogen 0.4 g/L. Lactate 7.8. Complete DIC.

The haematologist calls: 'She needs blood products NOW. How long has she been like this?'

The obstetric consultant arrives and looks at the CTG for two seconds. 'There is no fetal heartbeat. This baby needed delivering 25 minutes ago.'

outcome-excellent.text:
Category 1 CS under general anaesthesia.

Incision to delivery: 8 minutes.

A live male infant is delivered, 1.58kg. He is pale and floppy at delivery — Apgar 3 at 1 minute, 7 at 5 minutes. The neonatal team intubates briefly at 1 minute, extubates to CPAP by 3 minutes. Cord pH: 7.14 — acidotic but within the survivable range.

Uterus at delivery: A 6×8cm retroplacental haematoma is found adherent to the posterior uterine wall. Estimated total blood loss: 2100mL. Uterus contracts well after oxytocin bolus. No hysterectomy required.

MHP: 3 units pRBC transfused intraoperatively. Coagulation maintained — fibrinogen did not fall below 1.5 g/L. No further blood products required.

--- Final Results ---
Maternal: Transferred to HDU postoperatively Hb nadir 7.2 g/dL, transfused to 9.5 g/dL. Coags normalised by 24h. Discharged Day 6.
Neonatal: NICU Day 1–47. Graduated to nursery. Discharged home Day 52, breast-feeding established.
Cord pH at birth: 7.14 — within the survivable range. Neurology clear at 6-week follow-up.

Mohammed: 'The doctors at NICU say he might have some breathing problems for a few weeks but they think he'll be fine. Thank you.'

[!] Teaching Points:
• Placental abruption is a CLINICAL diagnosis — board-like uterus + dark haemorrhage + constant pain = abruption. USS confirms nothing when it's negative.
• Category III CTG = immediate delivery. There is no role for intrauterine resuscitation when the CTG pattern is already terminal.
• Major Haemorrhage Protocol (MHP) activation is life-saving — blood products run in parallel with the decision to deliver, not after
• At 31+5 weeks, baby survival with good NICU care is >95% — gestational age should not delay the decision to deliver when fetal compromise is present
• The 30-minute rule for Category 1 CS exists for a reason — it is achievable with a prepared team

outcome-survived-morbidity.text:
Category 1 CS under general anaesthesia.

Incision to delivery: 11 minutes.

A live male infant is delivered, 1.55kg. Apgar 1 at 1 minute, 5 at 5 minutes. He requires sustained positive-pressure ventilation and is intubated by the neonatal team. Cord pH: 7.01 — significant acidosis.

Uterus at delivery: A 7×9cm retroplacental haematoma. Uterus poorly contracted despite oxytocin — disseminated coagulopathy at this stage. Estimated blood loss: 3,400mL.

MHP ultimately activated intraoperatively: 8 units pRBC, 6 units FFP, 2 pools platelets, cryoprecipitate. Haematologist on the phone throughout. Uterine compression sutures placed. Balloon tamponade considered. Hysterectomy narrowly avoided.

--- Final Results ---
Maternal: ICU admission (72h). Hb nadir 5.8 g/dL. Acute kidney injury — creatinine peaked at 218 µmol/L, resolved by Day 8. DIC resolved with aggressive replacement. Discharged Day 11.
Neonatal: NICU Day 1–68. Cord pH 7.01 — neonatal encephalopathy protocol initiated, therapeutic hypothermia for 72 hours. Neurodevelopmental follow-up arranged. Feeding difficulties; nasogastric tube on discharge.
Patient discharged Day 11 without being able to hold her son — he remained in NICU.

[!] Teaching Points:
• Every minute of delay in a Category III CTG setting worsens fetal acidosis and the margin for intact survival narrows rapidly
• Cord pH is a direct marker of fetal hypoxic burden at delivery — the difference between 7.14 and 7.01 is the difference between normal neurodevelopment and uncertain outcome
• Major Haemorrhage Protocol must be activated BEFORE theatre, not when things go wrong on the table
• Intrauterine resuscitation is not treatment — it is a reason to delay the only treatment that actually works: delivery

outcome-fatal.text:
Crash Category 1 CS is performed.

Incision at 68 minutes after presentation.

A stillborn male infant is delivered. Weight 1.56kg. There is no cardiac activity at delivery. The cord pH cannot be obtained. Neonatal resuscitation is attempted for 20 minutes before the team stops.

The retroplacental clot weighs 820 grams. The majority of the placenta has separated.

Fatima develops catastrophic DIC intraoperatively: uncontrollable haemorrhage from all surfaces. Despite activation of the MHP, 22 units of blood products are administered. Peripartum hysterectomy is performed. She is transferred to ICU on vasopressors.

She survives, but requires renal replacement therapy for 11 days before her kidneys recover. She will not be able to carry a further pregnancy.

She is told about her son while still in ICU, 36 hours after the operation.

The case is reviewed at the Serious Incident panel. The primary finding: the delivery decision was delayed by a clinical escalation error. A Category III CTG was present from the moment monitoring was first applied. The 30-minute decision-to-delivery standard was missed by 38 minutes.

[!] Teaching Points:
• The Category 1 CS standard — 30 minutes from decision to delivery — is not a guideline. It is the physiological window within which intact fetal survival is achievable above a baseline rate.
• Category III CTG = NO DELAY. No blood results, no intrauterine resuscitation, no consent paperwork delays that cannot happen simultaneously.
• The blood results that prompted the wait were already predictable from the clinical picture. They changed nothing. They cost everything.
• DIC in major abruption is not a condition to wait for — it is a condition to pre-empt with MHP activation before it happens.
• Placental abruption is survivable for both mother and baby with fast, decisive, protocol-driven management. The tools exist. The barrier is recognition and speed.
